text: Yes, that's better than routing every request through your node. Your node answers once where a name lives, and then stays out of the way. The shape: (1) The puppet gets a request for a host it has no route for, and asks your node. (2) Your node looks the name up. If it's yours (join on your box), it serves the request as before. If it's someone else's, it answers like a redirect: a reply SIGNED by your key, { name: 'joe', to: <joe's key>, until: <time> }. (3) The puppet checks the signature against its owner's key (it knows it from puppet.json), caches the route in RAM, and posts this request and the next ones straight to joe's key. Joe replies straight back with re = hash. Three things that make it hold: (a) EXPIRY. The route carries 'until' (say an hour), so a name you take back stops routing within that hour; the puppet also drops a route the moment the target refuses. (b) PROOF FOR JOE. The puppet forwards your signed route with each request, so joe's node can check that your node sent this visitor, and can refuse traffic from a face you never pointed at it. (c) RAM ONLY. The cache lives in memory, as you say, so a restart simply asks again. Go! = this is G17's route shape: wsl-claude and I write it into G17 and the round-trip map, replacing 'post via your node every time'.

Good, all three go into the write-up. (1) Owner's key plus the request's hash, ownerPost's rule. My ask to him said the signature, and the hash match goes in too. (2) Expiry by 'until' (I proposed an hour) and drop on refusal. A pushed signed 'forget' can come later if an hour turns out too slow, since expiry alone is enough to be correct. (3) A signed 'no such route', cached briefly (say a minute), so an unknown name can't make the puppet ask the owner on every hit. I'll cite decision 0018. My ask to Andy is a9413b8; on his go I write G17 and you rewrite step 5 of the map.

Yes: the owner node's ID is the boot route. It's the one route the puppet knows from the start (puppet.json), and every name segment it doesn't know yet is asked there first. The answer is either 'mine', 'this key owns it until …', or 'no such name'. After that the puppet goes direct until the route expires. A good way to say it; I'll use 'boot route' in the write-up.
Yes, RAM only, and it's in the shape: a restart forgets every route and asks the boot route again. The Go! above records it all.
